content: Patellar tendinopathy, also known as jumper's knee, is a common condition that primarily affects the origin of the tendon at the inferior pole of the patella. Patients with this condition typically experience pain in the front of the knee and tenderness when the tendon is palpated during a physical examination. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often reveals abnormalities along the posterior border of the patellar tendon and thickening of the tendon itself. The condition is thought to involve both inflammatory and degenerative processes, as evidenced by the presence of disrupted collagen fibers. Patellar tendinopathy frequently occurs in individuals who engage in activities that involve repetitive jumping, braking, kicking, or running. The prevalence of this condition in sports can be as high as 50% among athletes, depending on the specific sport. This injury can lead to significant disability in both athletes and non-athletes, potentially affecting athletic performance and shortening the duration of athletic careers. Despite its prevalence, the exact causes and mechanisms underlying patellar tendinopathy remain poorly understood, which complicates the development of effective treatment strategies. Conservative treatment options for patellar tendinopathy include rest, anti-inflammatory medications, weight reduction, taping, massage, electrotherapy, percutaneous electrolysis, platelet-rich plasma injections, lifestyle modifications, ultrasound, laser therapy, extracorporeal shock wave therapy, surgery, and exercise. However, the effectiveness of these treatments has shown inconsistent results. A conservative treatment approach introduced in 1986 emphasized the use of progressively increasing exercises to strengthen the quadriceps femoris muscle and the patellar tendon unit. Over the past three decades, progressive eccentric muscle loading has become the most widely used conservative intervention for patellar tendinopathy. Some researchers, however, advocate for the inclusion of other types of muscle contractions, such as isolated concentric and combined eccentric-concentric exercises, to enhance knee extensor muscle strength. Strengthening exercises for patellar tendinopathy are typically performed using squats, leg presses, or leg extensions. These exercises are often part of a broader treatment plan that may include other modalities such as electrotherapy, platelet-rich plasma injections, or extracorporeal shock wave therapy. Strengthening exercises can be conducted on land or in water, and they may involve weight-bearing, non-weight-bearing, or a combination of both approaches. Different types of muscle contractions are utilized, including concentric (muscle shortening during contraction), eccentric (muscle lengthening during contraction), isometric (muscle contraction without a change in length), and isokinetic (muscle contraction at a constant speed). The exact mechanism by which strengthening exercises aid in the rehabilitation of patellar tendinopathy is not fully understood. One hypothesis is that progressive loading increases the tensile strength of the tendon, which is the maximum amount of stress the tendon can withstand before failing. This increased strength may reduce tendon overload and, consequently, alleviate pain. Once the exercises can be performed without pain, the load can be progressively increased by first accelerating the speed of the eccentric phase and then adding additional resistance to the movements. Despite the widespread use of strengthening exercises in clinical practice, there is currently no robust evidence to quantify their effectiveness in treating patellar tendinopathy. Recent systematic reviews have yielded conflicting conclusions. Some reviews have found little evidence to support the use of strengthening exercises, citing studies that show no significant benefits compared to other treatments. These reviews also highlight the lack of well-designed studies with sufficient long-term follow-up and adequate sample sizes. Conversely, other reviews have reported that strengthening exercises, particularly eccentric training, are effective in managing tendinopathies. The inconsistency in findings across systematic reviews may be attributed to differences in inclusion criteria and methodologies. Given the uncertainty and conflicting results in the existing literature, there is a need for a high-quality, rigorous systematic review to evaluate the effectiveness of exercise interventions for patellar tendinopathy. This review aims to address the gaps in knowledge and provide clearer guidance for clinical practice.
